triage.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
triage.reason: Common cause of unilateral leg swelling with clear risk factors; diagnosis reached by history, exam, D-dimer and ultrasound, with pulmonary embolism as a critical complication.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Incidence rises steadily with age, with most cases in adults over 60
Men and women are affected at similar rates overall
More common in Black adults than in White or Asian adults in US data
Often occurs during or shortly after a hospital stay or after surgery

risk_factors.text: Recent major surgery, especially hip or knee replacement
Prolonged immobility (bed rest, long-haul travel, cast immobilization)
Inherited thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C or S deficiency, antithrombin deficiency)
Combined oral contraceptive or hormone replacement therapy
Heart failure or recent myocardial infarction

family_history: Venous thromboembolism in a first-degree relative, especially before age 50
Known inherited thrombophilia in the family
social_history: Recent long-distance travel by plane, car or train
Prolonged bed rest or reduced mobility

chief_complaints.text: My left leg is swollen and achy
The calf is tender and feels warm
My leg hurts when I stand or walk
The skin on my leg looks red or discolored

hpi.onset: Gradual over hours to a few days; often noticed on waking or after a period of sitting still
hpi.duration: Usually present for 1-7 days at presentation
hpi.progression: Swelling and discomfort build over the first day or two, then plateau; may worsen with activity or dependency
hpi.location: Most often the calf or thigh of one leg; can involve the popliteal or femoral veins; upper extremity DVT occurs with central lines or effort thrombosis
hpi.radiation: Aching may extend up the inner thigh or into the groin; does not radiate down the leg in a dermatomal pattern
hpi.quality: Dull, heavy, tight or cramping ache; sometimes a pulling sensation in the calf
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate, typically 3-6/10; severe pain is unusual unless extensive iliofemoral thrombosis
hpi.timing: Constant, worse after standing or walking and better with elevation
aggravating: Prolonged sitting with the leg down
relieving: Analgesics such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen

associated_symptoms.text: Increased calf circumference compared with the other leg

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain or shortness of breath
Fever with chills and spreading skin redness
Recent leg trauma or muscle tear
Chronic venous insufficiency with skin staining and ulcers
Cellulitis with a clear portal of entry
Calf pain that is reproducible only with exercise and relieved by rest

positives.text: Redness or discoloration of the leg

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with only vague leg discomfort or worsening edema, and swelling can be attributed to chronic venous insufficiency or heart failure.
Leg swelling and discomfort are common in normal pregnancy, so DVT is often mistaken for normal pregnancy changes; left leg is more commonly affected due to compression of the left iliac vein.
Bilateral leg swelling and chronic skin changes are common, making asymmetry harder to detect and masking the classic unilateral presentation.
DVT is uncommon and usually occurs with central venous catheters, malignancy or inherited thrombophilia; presentation may be pain and swelling around a line or an extremity.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort, favors the affected leg, otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, in pain, reluctant to bear weight on the affected leg
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, tachypneic, or in shock (suggests massive iliofemoral thrombosis or pulmonary embolism)

findings.maneuver: Inspect both legs from groin to ankle with the patient standing or supine
findings.finding: Unilateral swelling of the calf, thigh, or entire leg

findings.maneuver: Measure the calf circumference 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity on both legs
findings.finding: Calf circumference increased by 3 cm or more on the affected side compared with the unaffected side

findings.maneuver: Palpate the calf muscles and along the deep veins
findings.finding: Tenderness over the calf or along the course of the deep veins

findings.maneuver: Compare skin temperature of both legs with the dorsum of the hand
findings.finding: Increased warmth over the affected leg

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin of both legs
findings.finding: Redness or discoloration over the affected leg

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the pretibial area and ankle for 5 seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the affected leg

findings.maneuver: Inspect the leg for dilated superficial veins
Palpate along the course of the superficial and deep veins
Passively dorsiflex the ankle with the knee slightly flexed

findings.finding: No swelling, tenderness, warmth, or erythema in the contralateral leg

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lungs and ask about chest pain or shortness of breath
findings.finding: Clear lungs, no pleuritic chest pain or dyspnea

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin for wounds, ulcers, or portals of entry
findings.finding: No open wound, draining ulcer, or interdigital fissure

findings.maneuver: Examine the knee and ankle joints
findings.finding: No joint swelling, effusion, or instability

findings.maneuver: Palpate the Achilles tendon and gastrocnemius muscle bellies
findings.finding: No focal tendon or muscle tenderness

labs.caveat: A negative D-dimer using a validated age-adjusted or highly sensitive assay makes DVT very unlikely and can rule it out in low-risk patients; a positive result is nonspecific and needs imaging. It is not useful when DVT is already highly likely.
Baseline coagulation testing before starting anticoagulation; a prolonged INR may reflect liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, or a lupus anticoagulant rather than the clot itself.
Baseline before heparin; a prolonged aPTT can also be seen with a lupus anticoagulant or factor deficiency.
Baseline platelet count before heparin; thrombocytopenia raises concern for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia or an underlying hematologic disorder.
Renal function guides choice and dosing of anticoagulants, especially low-molecular-weight heparin and direct oral anticoagulants.
Anemia may be from an underlying malignancy, chronic disease, or occult blood loss and affects anticoagulation safety.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and anticoagulation, since pregnancy changes both the diagnostic strategy and treatment.

findings.finding: Right axis deviation or right ventricular strain pattern suggesting pulmonary embolism

imaging.study: Compression ultrasound of the lower extremity veins
imaging.preferred_when: First-line test for suspected lower extremity DVT in all patients, including pregnancy

findings.text: Noncompressible deep vein (failure to collapse with probe pressure)
Thrombus visible within the vein lumen
Absent or reduced flow on color or spectral Doppler
Vein distended and enlarged compared with the adjacent artery
Nondiagnostic study because the deep veins are not adequately visualized

imaging.study: CT venography of the lower extremities with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When ultrasound is nondiagnostic or when iliac or pelvic vein thrombosis is suspected

findings.text: Filling defect within the deep vein lumen
Venous enlargement with surrounding soft tissue edema

imaging.study: MR venography of the lower extremities
imaging.preferred_when: When ultrasound and CT are inconclusive or contrast is contraindicated

findings.text: Filling defect or absent flow signal in the deep veins

imaging.preferred_when: When pulmonary embolism is suspected from symptoms or signs

findings.text: Filling defect in the pulmonary arteries

imaging.preferred_when: Pregnancy or contrast allergy when pulmonary embolism is suspected

initial.test: Compression ultrasound of the lower extremity veins
initial.why: First-line imaging to confirm or exclude DVT
initial.only_if: First-line imaging to confirm or exclude DVT

initial.why: Rules out DVT in low-risk patients when negative
initial.only_if: pretest probability is low and no high-risk features are present

initial.why: Baseline hemoglobin and platelet count before anticoagulation
Baseline renal function and electrolytes before anticoagulation
Baseline PT/INR and aPTT before starting heparin or warfarin
Rules out pregnancy before imaging and anticoagulation

supporting.test: CT venography of the lower extremities with IV contrast
supporting.why: Evaluates iliac or pelvic veins when ultrasound is nondiagnostic
supporting.only_if: ultrasound is nondiagnostic or iliac/pelvic vein thrombosis is suspected

supporting.test: MR venography of the lower extremities
supporting.why: Alternative when ultrasound and CT are inconclusive or contrast is contraindicated
supporting.only_if: ultrasound and CT are inconclusive or contrast is contraindicated
pulmonary embolism is suspected from dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxemia, or tachycardia

supporting.why: Looks for pulmonary embolism without iodinated contrast
supporting.only_if: pulmonary embolism is suspected and the patient is pregnant or has a contrast allergy

supporting.why: May identify an inherited or acquired thrombophilia
supporting.only_if: unprovoked DVT in a young patient, strong family history, recurrent VTE, or unusual site

supporting.why: Unprovoked DVT can be the first sign of occult malignancy
supporting.only_if: DVT is unprovoked and cancer screening is not up to date

not_indicated.why: Not indicated unless pulmonary embolism is suspected

decision_points: Use a validated clinical probability score (Wells or Geneva) before ordering D-dimer or ultrasound
In low-probability patients, a negative highly sensitive or age-adjusted D-dimer excludes DVT without imaging
In moderate- or high-probability patients, go straight to compression ultrasound
If the initial ultrasound is negative but suspicion remains high, repeat ultrasound in 5-7 days or check D-dimer
Pregnancy test before CT or anticoagulation in anyone who could be pregnant
Assess for pulmonary embolism symptoms and hemodynamic instability at every step

criteria.name: Wells score for DVT
criteria.summary: A clinical probability tool that assigns points for active cancer, paralysis or recent cast immobilization, bed rest or major surgery within 4 weeks, tenderness along deep veins, entire-leg swelling, calf swelling 3 cm or more greater than the other leg, pitting edema, collateral superficial veins, prior DVT, and an alternative diagnosis at least as likely. The total stratifies patients into low, moderate, or high probability and guides D-dimer and ultrasound use.
items: Paralysis, paresis, or recent plaster immobilization of the lower extremity
Bedridden for more than 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks
Localized tenderness along the distribution of the deep venous system
Calf swelling 3 cm or more compared with the asymptomatic leg
Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg
Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: DVT and pulmonary embolism are the same disease process; a clot can break loose and travel to the lungs, and patients with DVT may already have a silent or symptomatic PE.
differential.trigger: Any new dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, or syncope in a patient with leg swelling

history: Sudden shortness of breath
Pleuritic chest pain worse with inspiration
Coughing up blood
Lightheadedness or syncope
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to the leg findings
Tachypnea
Hypoxemia on pulse oximetry
Signs of right heart strain such as a loud P2 or elevated JVP
labs: Elevated troponin or BNP suggesting right ventricular strain
imaging: Filling defect in the pulmonary arteries on CT pulmonary angiography
Mismatched segmental perfusion defect on V/Q scan
Right ventricular enlargement on echocardiography or CT
ecg: Right axis deviation or right bundle branch block

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Unilateral leg redness, warmth, swelling, and pain are the classic shared presentation of cellulitis and DVT.
differential.trigger: Fever, chills, a clear portal of entry such as a wound or interdigital fissure, or rapidly spreading erythema

history: Fever and chills
Rapidly spreading redness
Recent skin break, insect bite, or fungal foot infection
Pain is more superficial and burning
exam: Well-demarcated, spreading erythema with a leading edge
Warm, tender, indurated skin
Lymphangitic streaking
Regional lymphadenopathy
imaging: Ultrasound shows subcutaneous edema and no deep vein thrombus
MRI may show skin and subcutaneous inflammation without venous filling defect

differential.name: Baker cyst rupture
differential.why_considered: Rupture of a popliteal cyst causes acute calf pain, swelling, and a positive Homans sign, closely mimicking DVT.

history: Sudden onset of calf pain, often after activity
Known knee osteoarthritis or meniscal tear
Pain and swelling behind the knee
No DVT risk factors
exam: Tenderness and fullness in the popliteal fossa
Knee effusion or joint line tenderness
Crescent-shaped ecchymosis near the ankle or medial malleolus
labs: D-dimer may be mildly elevated but is nonspecific
imaging: Ultrasound shows a popliteal cyst with fluid dissection into the calf and a compressible deep venous system
MRI demonstrates the cyst and surrounding fluid without a venous filling defect

differential.name: Gastrocnemius or soleus muscle tear
differential.why_considered: A calf muscle strain or tear produces acute calf pain, swelling, and tenderness that can be mistaken for DVT.

history: Sudden onset during exercise or a specific movement
Audible pop or snap at the time of injury
Pain is focal and worse with muscle contraction
No immobilization or thrombotic risk factors
exam: Focal tenderness over the medial gastrocnemius
Pain reproduced by resisted plantar flexion or passive stretching
Ecchymosis may appear after 24-48 hours
imaging: Ultrasound shows muscle fiber disruption, hematoma, or fluid collection with normal compressible deep veins
MRI demonstrates muscle edema or tear without venous thrombus

differential.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
differential.why_considered: Chronic venous disease causes leg swelling, aching, and skin discoloration, and can be mistaken for an acute DVT, especially in older adults.

history: Longstanding, slowly progressive leg heaviness and swelling
Symptoms worse at the end of the day and with prolonged standing
History of varicose veins or prior leg surgery
No acute onset or thrombotic risk factors
exam: Bilateral or symmetric lower extremity edema
Brown hemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis, or stasis ulcers near the ankle
Varicose veins
No acute warmth or focal deep vein tenderness
imaging: Venous duplex shows venous reflux and a compressible deep venous system without acute thrombus

differential.name: Lymphedema
differential.why_considered: Lymphedema causes unilateral or asymmetric leg swelling that can be confused with DVT, particularly after cancer treatment or surgery.

history: Gradual, progressive swelling over weeks to months
History of lymph node dissection, radiation, or filariasis
Swelling is firm and nonpitting
No acute pain or warmth
exam: Nonpitting, firm edema
Positive Stemmer sign (inability to pinch the dorsal foot skin)
Thickened skin with a peau d'orange appearance
No erythema or deep vein tenderness
imaging: Venous duplex shows normal compressible deep veins
Lymphoscintigraphy may show impaired lymphatic drainage

differential.name: Superficial thrombophlebitis
differential.why_considered: Inflammation and thrombosis of a superficial vein cause a tender, red, warm cord that can be mistaken for DVT.

history: Tenderness and redness along a superficial vein
Recent IV catheter or infusion
Varicose veins
Pain is superficial and follows a linear track
exam: Palpable, tender, cord-like superficial vein
Erythema in a linear distribution
No significant calf or thigh swelling
imaging: Ultrasound shows thrombus within a superficial vein with a normal deep venous system

severity.mild: Distal (calf) DVT with minimal swelling, mild discomfort, no functional limitation, and no evidence of pulmonary embolism
severity.moderate: Proximal (popliteal, femoral, or iliac) DVT with marked unilateral swelling, pain limiting ambulation, and no hemodynamic or respiratory compromise
severity.severe: Extensive iliofemoral DVT with severe pain, marked swelling, risk of venous gangrene, or concurrent submassive pulmonary embolism with right ventricular strain but stable blood pressure
severity.critical: Massive iliofemoral DVT with phlegmasia cerulea dolens or venous gangrene, or concurrent massive pulmonary embolism with hypotension, shock, or cardiac arrest

red_flags.finding: Sudden shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, or hemoptysis
red_flags.meaning: Suggests pulmonary embolism; needs urgent evaluation and anticoagulation
Suggests massive pulmonary embolism or hemodynamic compromise; emergency intervention required
Suggests pulmonary embolism or right heart strain

red_flags.finding: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (painful, blue, tense leg with absent pulses)
red_flags.meaning: Impending venous gangrene; requires urgent vascular intervention

red_flags.finding: Rapidly progressive swelling with compartment syndrome signs
red_flags.meaning: Severe venous hypertension and possible tissue necrosis

red_flags.finding: Fever with chills and spreading erythema
red_flags.meaning: Suggests cellulitis or septic thrombophlebitis rather than uncomplicated DVT

complications.name: Recurrent venous thromboembolism
clues: New leg swelling or chest symptoms after stopping anticoagulation

complications.name: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens and venous gangrene
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
clues: Platelet count drop by more than 50% after starting heparin
Skin necrosis at heparin injection sites

special_populations.differences: DVT is more common in pregnancy and the postpartum period, especially in the left leg due to compression of the left iliac vein. Swelling and discomfort are common in normal pregnancy, so a high index of suspicion is needed. Low-molecular-weight heparin is the preferred anticoagulant; warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants are avoided. Compression ultrasound is first-line imaging.

May present with vague leg discomfort or worsening edema attributed to chronic venous insufficiency or heart failure. Higher risk of bleeding on anticoagulation and more likely to have comorbid cancer or immobility.

Bilateral leg swelling and chronic skin changes are common, making asymmetry harder to detect. Weight-based dosing of low-molecular-weight heparin is challenging, and direct oral anticoagulants may be preferred.

DVT is uncommon and usually associated with central venous catheters, malignancy, or inherited thrombophilia. Presentation may be pain and swelling around a line or an extremity. Anticoagulation is specialist-directed.

Low-molecular-weight heparin and direct oral anticoagulants require dose adjustment or avoidance depending on the degree of renal impairment. Unfractionated heparin may be preferred when renal function is severely reduced.
Higher risk of infection and septic thrombophlebitis; fever and systemic signs should prompt evaluation for an infectious source in addition to DVT.

key_questions.question: When did the leg swelling and pain start, and how has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over hours to a few days, building then plateauing; acute onset during exertion suggests a muscle tear

key_questions.question: Is the swelling in one leg or both?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral; bilateral swelling points to heart failure, venous insufficiency, or lymphedema

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the swelling and pain — calf, thigh, or the whole leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Calf or thigh; entire-leg or thigh involvement suggests proximal (iliofemoral) thrombosis

key_questions.question: What makes it better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with standing, walking, or dependency and better with elevation and rest

key_questions.question: Have you had any chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughed up blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Any of these suggests concurrent pulmonary embolism and changes urgency

key_questions.question: Have you had surgery, been hospitalized, or been on bed rest in the last 3 months?
key_questions.looking_for: Major surgery (especially hip or knee replacement) or immobility within 12 weeks is a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you had a blood clot in the leg or lung before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior venous thromboembolism markedly raises the probability of recurrence

key_questions.question: Do you have cancer, or are you being treated for cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: Active malignancy or chemotherapy is a strong provoking factor

key_questions.question: Have you been on a long trip or sitting still for many hours recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-haul travel or prolonged sitting with the legs dependent

key_questions.question: Do you take birth control pills, estrogen, tamoxifen, or raloxifene?
key_questions.looking_for: Hormonal or selective estrogen receptor modulator therapy raises clot risk

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy or the postpartum period increases risk and changes imaging and treatment choices

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a blood clot, especially before age 50?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of venous thromboembolism or a known inherited thrombophilia

key_questions.question: Have you had recent leg trauma, a muscle injury, or a cast or brace on the leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Trauma or immobilization can cause a muscle tear or provoke a clot

key_questions.question: Do you have any wounds, ulcers, or fungal infection between the toes?
key_questions.looking_for: A portal of entry suggests cellulitis rather than DVT

key_questions.question: Any fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: High fever with chills favors cellulitis or septic thrombophlebitis

key_questions.question: Do you smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking is a weak additional risk factor

reasoning_points: Unilateral leg swelling with calf tenderness, warmth, and a measurable calf circumference difference
Presence of provoking risk factors such as recent surgery, immobility, active cancer, prior VTE, pregnancy, or estrogen therapy
Clinical probability assessed with a validated score (Wells or Geneva) before testing
D-dimer used only to rule out DVT in low-probability patients; a negative highly sensitive or age-adjusted result excludes it
Compression ultrasound is the first-line confirmatory test, showing a noncompressible deep vein or intraluminal thrombus
Pregnancy excluded before imaging and anticoagulation in anyone who could be pregnant
Pulmonary embolism considered and assessed at every step, since DVT and PE are the same disease process
Alternative diagnoses such as cellulitis, Baker cyst rupture, muscle tear, chronic venous insufficiency, lymphedema, and superficial thrombophlebitis weighed and addressed

easy: Classic unilateral calf swelling and tenderness after recent surgery or prolonged immobility
Clear calf circumference difference of 3 cm or more with warmth and erythema
No chest symptoms and normal vital signs
Compression ultrasound confirms a noncompressible popliteal or femoral vein
medium: Woman of reproductive age on combined oral contraceptives with unilateral leg swelling
Older adult whose swelling is attributed to chronic venous insufficiency or heart failure
Mildly elevated D-dimer in a low-probability patient requiring imaging to sort out
Upper extremity DVT associated with a central venous catheter
Concurrent cellulitis concern with fever and leg redness
hard: Pregnant patient with leg swelling that overlaps normal pregnancy changes
Obesity with bilateral chronic edema masking asymmetry
Baker cyst rupture or gastrocnemius tear mimicking DVT with a positive Homans sign
Patient with concurrent pulmonary embolism presenting with dyspnea or syncope
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens with a tense, blue, painful leg and absent pulses
Renal impairment complicating anticoagulant selection and dosing
